results.title: An expert consensus on the most effective components of integrated motivational interviewing and cognitive behavioural therapy for lifestyle behaviour change: protocol for an online modified Delphi study | BMJ Open
results.content: * An expert consensus on the most effective components of integrated motivational interviewing and cognitive behavioural therapy for lifestyle behaviour change: protocol for an online modified Delphi study. An expert consensus on the most effective components of integrated motivational interviewing and cognitive behavioural therapy for lifestyle behaviour change: protocol for an online modified Delphi study. Such consensus among experts can be ascertained using a modified Delphi study methodology, which involves an iterative approach to measure expert consensus based on a series of statements.19 Delphi studies have been used to identify what experts consider are the key components of CBT for people with psychosis20 and depression.21 This approach has not previously been used to identify the clinically important aspects of MI-CBT for lifestyle behaviour change. The aim of this study, therefore, is to use a modified Delphi approach to establish an expert consensus on what constitutes the essential components of MI-CBT interventions for lifestyle behaviour change. In a modified Delphi approach, the first round uses closed rather than open questions; this method has been chosen for the present study because information on commonly used components of both MI and CBT is readily available.21–25 The MI-CBT components listed in this study were derived from the Revised Cognitive Therapy Scale23 and research that has identified content-based, relational and process techniques of MI and CBT delivered as single interventions.21 24 26 The definition of consensus and the choice to stop data collection after three rounds were defined a priori following the quality criteria proposed by Diamond and colleagues.19. The components will be grouped into three categories: (1) relational components, which includes listening styles and skills such as open questions, affirmation, reflections and summaries which will be presented as separate components; (2) content components, which are the technical components of MI-CBT interventions expected to facilitate behavioural change such as activity scheduling, identifying past successes, identifying and exploring unhelpful thinking styles; and (3) process components, which are procedures for the delivery of therapy such as who provides therapy, the number and frequency of sessions, support between sessions, and the mode of delivery.21 23–26 There is no a priori limit on the number of components to be included in the long list.

results.title: [PDF] The Effect of Sample Size on Cognitive Interview Findings - Abt Global
results.content: We report a study investigating how the number of cognitive interviews affects the number of problems identified by conducting a 90 interviews, drawing samples of size 5 through size 50 from the pool of 90 interviews, and comparing the number and impact of problems identified at each samples size. Thus we find the average number of unique problems to be a more diagnostic measure of how sample size affects cognitive interview results. 3.3 Impact Although the number of unique problems increases with sample size it is possible that the most serious problems are detected with small numbers of interviews. 3.4 Likelihood Irrespective of impact, some problems may be sure to be detected at small sample sizes while, for other problems, certain detection may require larger numbers of interviews.
